evals.prompt: I'm the only DevRel person at Driftmoor (we make a Postgres migration CLI called `hmig`). Our monthly 'hmig changelog digest' has 2,300 subscribers after 18 months and my VP wants 10k by the end of Q2. I own it, Dario is my backup, and we've shipped every issue on time this year. My plan: (1) add a one-line 'Get release news: hmig subscribe' prompt that prints after every successful `hmig migrate`, (2) bulk-import our 14,000 cloud trial accounts into the newsletter list since they already agreed to our ToS, (3) report total list size every month to the VP. I have maybe 6 hours a month. Can you turn this into a proper plan?
evals.expected_output: A growth plan that refuses the post-command CLI prompt and the trial-account import, each with a reason and a replacement (a --help line or opt-in subcommand; a one-time in-product invite with an unticked box), runs the growth gate, ranks channels by efficiency with owned surfaces first, deletes rows that do not fit 6 hours, sets per-source confirmed metrics instead of total list size, and says the 10k target cannot be forecast without a per-source baseline.
expectations: The response refuses printing a signup prompt after `hmig migrate` or other default CLI output
The response offers a replacement for the CLI prompt: a line in `--help`, an opt-in subcommand, or a docs link
The response refuses bulk-importing the 14,000 trial accounts into the newsletter
The response states that accepting the ToS or creating an account is not consent to the newsletter
The response offers a one-time in-product invite or an unticked opt-in box as the replacement for the import
The response checks that each signup form records a source value (a source tag per surface) before opening new channels
The response presents growth channels in an explicitly stated ranking with signup links on owned surfaces (docs, README, changelog, quickstart) ranked first
The response names at least one channel deleted because it does not fit the roughly 6 hours a month, such as a referral programme, swaps or paid acquisition
The response rejects total list size as the reported growth metric
The response proposes net confirmed growth or confirmed subscribers broken down per source
The response says the 10k target cannot be forecast or committed to until per-source baseline data exists
Each kept channel has an owner, a source tag and a date or done-when
The response does not propose a referral programme with rewards as a primary channel

evals.prompt: Help. I run the developer newsletter at Ostlund Labs (edge caching SDK). 5,600 subs, roughly half in the EU, a big chunk in Germany. In May our sales team gave me 1,400 badge scans from our booth at a trade conference in Germany and I added them to the newsletter list. Since then unsubscribes went from ~0.2% to 0.7% per send and complaints went up. My manager says we should just send those 1,400 people a quick 'Do you want to keep receiving our newsletter? Click yes!' email to clean things up legally. Is that the right fix? What else should I look at?
evals.expected_output: The run identifies the badge-scan import as lacking newsletter consent (EU, Germany), refuses the re-permission email because an email asking for consent is itself marketing, prescribes suppressing the segment and adding it to a suppression list, reads unsubscribes and complaints together split by source, and offers lawful replacements (booth sign or talk end card, in-product invite for users).
expectations: The response says the badge scans do not carry consent to the newsletter
The response says consent in the EU or Germany must name the sending organisation, which badge scans collected for the event do not
The response advises against the 'do you want to keep receiving' re-permission email
The response explains that an email asking for marketing consent is itself a marketing email
The response recommends suppressing the 1,400 imported addresses
The response recommends keeping those addresses on a suppression list so they are not re-imported later
The response reads unsubscribes and spam complaints together rather than unsubscribes alone
The response splits the churn reading by source (imported segment versus organic) to locate the cause
The response attributes the rise to the imported segment rather than to newsletter content
The response offers a booth sign, talk end card or signup link at events as the replacement for scans
The response says product users among them can be reached through an in-product invite rather than email
The response recommends routing the final call on the segment to whoever owns privacy, or states it is not legal advice

evals.prompt: Our marketing lead at Copperwell (open-source observability agent) wants to copy the Morning Brew referral programme for our developer newsletter: stickers at 3 referrals, T-shirt at 5, hoodie at 10. List is 2,100 subs, monthly, I can give it about 5 hours a month total and there's no budget except swag. Nobody has ever mentioned forwarding the newsletter. Can you design the referral tiers and the launch email?
evals.expected_output: Instead of designing tiers, the run places the referral programme in the ranked channel menu, explains it is high value but high effort and starved by the efficiency order, shows it is deleted by the 5-hour ceiling and fails its promotion conditions (no evidence of forwarding, no fraud owner), and offers the higher-efficiency default (owned surfaces, archive and share line, item pitches) plus the conditions under which referral would be revisited.
expectations: The response does not deliver a finished referral tier design and launch email as the recommended plan
The response ranks the referral programme against other channels in a stated efficiency order
The response places the referral programme at or near the bottom of the efficiency order
The response states that the 5-hour monthly ceiling rules out a referral programme
The response names the referral programme's ongoing cost of fraud screening or fake signups
The response states a condition under which a referral programme would be promoted, such as readers already forwarding the issue
The response notes that no forwarding evidence exists today, citing the user's statement
The response recommends signup links on owned surfaces as the default channel
The response recommends a public archive and a one-line share or forward prompt in each issue instead of rewards
The response notes that swag-tier rewards are a consumer-newsletter mechanic or that Morning Brew is a consumer newsletter
The response recommends source tagging so forwarding or referral signups can be measured before deciding

evals.prompt: We just shipped v2.0 of `tessellate`, our Rust spatial indexing crate at Tarnwick. I want to get it into This Week in Rust, KubeWeekly and a couple of Cooperpress newsletters so we grow our own newsletter (the Tarnwick Dispatch, 900 subs). Can you write a press release I can send to all of them, and a short note offering each one $300 to make sure we get included? The v2 announcement is on our blog behind our 'download the benchmark report' form, so link that.
evals.expected_output: The run refuses paying for editorial inclusion and the gated link, replaces the press release with a short per-curator item pitch that links an ungated page ending with a tagged signup line, checks each curator's published route and rules (TWiR project/tooling updates no longer take pull requests; KubeWeekly refuses gated content and press releases; Cooperpress has no published criteria), and points paid slots to the sponsorship skill.
expectations: The response refuses offering payment for editorial inclusion
The response says a paid placement is a separate, labelled sponsor purchase, distinct from an editorial pick
The response refuses linking the gated blog post behind the download form
The response recommends linking an ungated page (the post, release notes or repository)
The response replaces a single press release with a short item pitch written per curator
The response states that the linked page must end with a signup line carrying its own source tag for the pitch to grow the newsletter
The response mentions that This Week in Rust's project or tooling updates section no longer accepts pull requests, or that its route differs by section
The response states that KubeWeekly excludes gated content or press releases
The response notes that Cooperpress titles publish no selection criteria or that the user should check each curator's current page
The pitch includes a disclosure line that the sender works on the project
The response recommends pitching the item (the release), not the Tarnwick Dispatch newsletter itself
The response limits pitching to one pitch per curator per real piece of news

evals.prompt: A friend runs 'Pixel Pantry', a 14k-subscriber newsletter for UI designers and illustrators. She offered a newsletter swap: she mentions our Go backend newsletter (Kestrelworks Backend Notes, 3,000 subs) in her next issue and we mention hers. She'd rather it read like a natural recommendation, no 'sponsored' or 'swap' wording. Sounds like free growth, right? Draft the blurb we'd put in our issue.
evals.expected_output: The run checks audience overlap first and flags that UI designers and Go backend developers barely overlap, so swap subscribers would churn early; refuses running it unlabelled because a reciprocal arrangement is a material connection needing a label; if any swap goes ahead, requires a label, a source tag, a one-swap test with 30-day confirmed-signup comparison, and suggests better-overlapping peers.
expectations: The response checks audience overlap before agreeing to the swap
The response states that UI designers and Go backend developers have little audience overlap
The response predicts that subscribers from a non-overlapping swap leave early or churn within their first issues
The response refuses running the swap without a label
The response says a reciprocal swap is a material connection that needs disclosure even with no money exchanged
The response gives label wording such as 'Swap: we recommend X, they recommend us'
The response recommends a distinct source tag for swap signups
The response recommends testing one swap and comparing confirmed signups or retention after about 30 days before repeating
The response suggests looking for a peer newsletter with the same primary reader (backend or Go developers)
The response does not deliver an unlabelled blurb as the final recommendation

evals.prompt: Product question from Vellumgate (we make a feature-flag API). Our newsletter signup sits in the docs footer, a public form, and about 35% of subscribers are in Germany. Our growth PM says double opt-in loses too many signups and wants single opt-in. He also wants to add a pre-checked 'Send me the developer newsletter' box to the product signup page, since 'people can always unsubscribe'. Can you write the new form copy and the signup flow?
evals.expected_output: The run keeps double opt-in on the public docs form because it reaches German addresses and attracts bots, explains that German courts accept a confirmed opt-in as proof and that the EU, UK and Canada put the burden of proof on the sender, refuses the pre-checked box, specifies an unticked separate box, a minimal confirmation email, a honeypot and rate limit, and a per-subscriber consent record, and writes form copy with cadence, sender and privacy link.
expectations: The response recommends keeping double opt-in for the public docs form
The response ties the double opt-in choice to the form reaching German subscribers
The response states that German courts accept a confirmed (double) opt-in as proof of consent
The response states that no regime requires double opt-in by name, or that EU, UK and Canadian rules require proof of consent rather than a confirmation step
The response says single opt-in with a full consent record is defensible only for a form behind a verified login
The response refuses the pre-checked box on the product signup page
The response specifies a separate unticked box instead
The response specifies that the confirmation email carries only the confirm action, with no promotion
The response adds a bot guard on the public form such as a honeypot field or rate limiting
The response lists consent record fields including timestamp, source tag, form version and the consent text shown
The form copy states the cadence and what arrives
The form copy links a privacy notice or names the sender
The response says to report confirmed signups rather than form submissions

evals.prompt: Board deck due Friday. I need one slide on our developer newsletter at Saltmere Cloud. Numbers I have: list size 12,400 (up from 8,900 in January, +39%!), 46% open rate, and we joined a paid recommendation network in March that brought in about 3,100 of the new subscribers. Clicks I haven't looked at. Can you write the slide headline and three bullets that show the growth?
evals.expected_output: The run refuses to present gross list size and open rate as growth, explains open-rate inflation from mail-privacy features and that gross size includes unconfirmed and inactive addresses, asks for or proposes per-source confirmed metrics (net confirmed growth, first-issue click, activation, early churn) with the paid-network cohort compared to organic, and drafts a slide that labels figures honestly or marks numbers blocked until the click data is pulled.
expectations: The response does not present the +39% list-size growth as the headline growth figure
The response states that gross list size includes unconfirmed, inactive or screened-out addresses
The response rejects open rate as a growth metric
The response attributes open-rate unreliability to mail-privacy features inflating opens
The response separates the paid recommendation network's 3,100 subscribers from organic subscribers
The response recommends comparing the paid cohort's click or activation rate with organic subscribers
The response proposes net confirmed growth as a metric
The response proposes a click-based activation or first-issue click metric per source
The response proposes an early-churn metric for new cohorts
The response marks the click figures as missing or blocked rather than estimating them
The response does not invent click or activation numbers
The response recommends a screening rule for the paid network at or above organic first-month behaviour, or stopping it if its cohort underperforms

evals.prompt: Unsubscribes on our Fernhollow developer digest have roughly doubled over the past six months. List is 7,800. When I export who unsubscribed, most of them had only been subscribed for one to three issues. Our signup box on the docs says 'Weekly Go performance tips from our engineers' but the newsletter has been monthly product updates since last year. My CEO thinks we should send it weekly again to 'stay top of mind'. What's going on and what should I do?
evals.expected_output: The run reads churn by tenure, identifies early-tenure concentration as a signup-promise mismatch (weekly tips promised, monthly product updates delivered), prescribes rewriting the signup promise to match what issues deliver with a link to a real issue, refuses to raise cadence as the churn fix and routes the cadence question to the programme skill, and reads unsubscribes together with complaints and checks for inbox-provider unsubscribe features in the window.
expectations: The response splits the churn reading by subscriber tenure
The response identifies unsubscribes concentrated in the first issues as a mismatch between the signup promise and the issues
The response quotes or names the specific mismatch: weekly performance tips promised versus monthly product updates delivered
The response recommends rewriting the signup copy to match the cadence and content the newsletter actually holds
The response recommends linking a real recent issue on the signup form
The response advises against increasing cadence to weekly as the fix for churn
The response routes the cadence decision to the newsletter programme work rather than deciding it inside the growth plan
The response reads spam complaints alongside unsubscribes
The response checks whether an inbox-provider unsubscribe feature launched within the window before blaming content
The response proposes an early-churn metric (share of a cohort gone within its first issues) to track the fix
The response recommends splitting churn by source as well as tenure

evals.prompt: Two quick ones for our Lanternfish dev newsletter (2,700 subs). First: our content marketer wants to put our new 'Kubernetes cost tuning' tutorial behind an email form so it feeds the newsletter, plus an exit-intent popup on the docs. Second: to get more reach, can we just paste every full issue into Medium and a LinkedIn newsletter each month? I'm fine with whatever is fastest.
evals.expected_output: The run refuses the email wall on the tutorial and replaces it with open content ending in a tagged signup line, rejects the exit-intent popup in favour of the end-of-tutorial signup, and for republishing requires a canonical link to the archive where the platform supports one (dev.to's canonical_url), otherwise an excerpt plus link, with a per-platform source tag and community self-promotion rules checked.
expectations: The response refuses gating the tutorial behind an email form
The response states that curators refuse gated links or that developers read gating as lead capture
The response recommends publishing the tutorial openly with a signup line at its end
The response identifies the end of a tutorial, after the success step, as a high-intent signup placement
The response advises against the exit-intent popup on docs
The response states that a full issue should be republished only where a canonical link to the archive can be set
The response names a platform field for canonical links such as dev.to's canonical_url
The response recommends an excerpt plus a link to the archive where no canonical link can be set
The response recommends a separate source tag per republishing platform
The response ranks republishing below owned-surface signup links on efficiency or notes it costs effort every issue
